title: How to explain a new policy with a short animated video
summary: Explain a new policy or safety procedure in a 60–120 second animated video without knowing how to create and edit videos.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- Decide four things before scripting: what changes, who it applies to, what people will do differently, and the one action you need by a date.
- Keep it to 60–120 seconds (about 130–260 words of narration) in six beats: what's changing, who it covers, before and after, what stays the same, what to do now, and where to ask.
- Put rules and numbers on screen as text and icons, give a procedure a numbered step counter, and save characters for policies about behavior.
- Caption and translate the whole video, then check understanding with one question about the change and the behavior it was meant to change.[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) builds the video from your policy document or a prompt, and you update it by editing the line that changed.


Policy changes often reach employees as a PDF attached to an email, with a box to tick that says they've read it. Ask five of them a week later what they now do differently, and most of us won't be able to.


A 60- to 120-second animated video closes that gap when it's built around the change instead of the document. Most of the work happens before anyone opens a video tool, so this guide starts with four decisions, then covers the structure, script, visuals, and accessibility, and how to check that people understood. The same method works for a safety procedure.


## What is a policy explainer video?


A policy explainer video is a short animated video, usually 60 to 120 seconds, that tells employees what a new policy or procedure changes, who it applies to, what they must do differently, and by when. Motion graphics and on-screen text carry the facts, and the video points to the full policy instead of replacing it.


The policy document and the[compliance course](https://www.clueso.io/use-cases/compliance-training-videos) stay the record. The explainer covers only the part someone would get wrong on Monday if nobody told them, and for a safety procedure, that part is a sequence of steps.


This guide is about explaining one change well. If you're turning a whole handbook into a set of short videos and keeping them current, our guide to[employee handbook training videos](https://www.clueso.io/blog/employee-handbook-training-videos) covers which sections to film and how to maintain the library.


## What should you decide before anyone writes the script?


An explainer has to leave most of the policy out, so these four calls belong to whoever owns the policy, not whoever makes the video.


**What changes.** Write each change as a before-and-after pair. "Report sickness by calling your manager" becomes "Report sickness in the app before your shift starts." Leave out the clauses that didn't change, even the ones legal spent longest on.


**Who it affects.** Name the groups and the exceptions in one sentence, like "everyone on hourly contracts, except night-route drivers." If two groups have to do different things, make two videos.


**What they'll do differently.** Turn each change into something a person does or stops doing. "Don't forward customer files to a personal email address" gives a viewer something to act on, and a line about "strengthening our approach to data security" doesn't.


**The one action you need.** Pick the single thing every viewer must do, with a date, such as "update the app before January 1." That line becomes the last scene.


## How should you structure a 60- to 120-second policy video?


At the 130 words per minute our[guide to training video length](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-long-should-a-training-video-be) uses, 60 to 120 seconds holds 130 to 260 words of narration. The median video exported from Clueso over the past year ran 91 seconds, across 26,610 videos. Six beats fit in that length, in this order:


Beat


Time


What's on screen


What's changing, and when


0–10s


The date, large, and the number of changes


Who it covers


10–20s


An icon for each group, with exceptions crossed out


Before and after


20–60s


One change per scene, the old rule struck through as the new one appears


What stays the same


60–75s


A checklist of what didn't change


What to do now


75–100s


The action under its deadline


Where to ask


100–120s


Where the full policy lives and who answers questions


Keep the "what stays the same" beat when time is tight. People hearing about a new leave policy want to know whether their allowance shrank, and five seconds on screen answers that before anyone messages HR.


*What's changed in our leave policy: a sample video made in Clueso for a fictional freight company. Each change gets its own card, then "What stays the same", then what to do before January 1. An AI avatar presents, but the on-screen text carries every fact.*


## What should the script say, and what should it never paraphrase?


If you build the video from the policy document, the first draft of the script comes from the document itself. Your job is to check it against the four decisions.


**Keep numbers and defined terms exactly as the policy states them.** "Four weeks' notice" never becomes "about a month", and "authorized person" stays "authorized person", because that's the phrase an auditor will look for.


**Say the action in the imperative.** "Report sickness in the app" is easier to act on than "Employees are now expected to use the app for absence reporting."


**Read it aloud to someone outside the team.** If they can repeat the action and the date after one listen, the script is ready.


A two-change leave policy written to that pattern runs about 80 words:


> From January 1, two things change about how you take leave. This applies to everyone on hourly contracts. First, between November and December, book leave four weeks ahead, up from two. Second, report sick days in the app before your shift starts. Your allowance and your sick pay stay the same. Before January 1, update the app and check that you can log in. The full policy is in the app under Policies, and the People team can answer questions.


## Which visuals work best for a policy or procedure explainer?


Choose the visual by what the viewer has to do with the information. A talking head rarely helps, because the presenter takes up the space where the rule should be.


What you're explaining


Visual that works


A rule or a number, like a notice period


Kinetic text and icons, the new number large and the old one struck through


Who qualifies


An icon or silhouette for each group, with exceptions crossed out


A procedure with a fixed order


A flat or isometric scene of the equipment, with a step counter pinned to a corner


A judgment call, like spotting phishing


A short story with characters, or comic panels


A timeline, like leave or a phased return


A calendar or bar that fills week by week


Keep one style across the series, so the next video from HR looks like it belongs with the last one. If your company is used to hearing from a person, an[AI avatar](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-avatars) can open the video, with the facts on screen beside it. None of this needs a designer, because[motion graphics](https://www.clueso.io/tools/motion-graphics) and[kinetic text](https://www.clueso.io/tools/text-animation) can be generated from a prompt.


*How parental leave works: a sample made in Clueso for a fictional hotel group, in paper cut-out. Each fact gets a label, like "16 paid weeks". Then the video stops to ask which of two timelines applies to a colleague named Tom.*


*The email that looked real: a sample made in Clueso for a fictional insurer, in comic panels. The viewer gets a few seconds to find five red flags in a payment request. The video ends on one action: report it with the button in your toolbar.*


## How do you explain a safety procedure step by step?


A safety procedure has something most policy changes don't: an order people must follow. If someone skips the step that releases stored energy, a press that's locked out can still move.


**Keep one procedure on one machine per video.** A safety and training lead at an equipment rental company described what he wanted to us in November: "This is a skid steer. This is how to get into a skid steer. That's it." His certification courses already run for hours or days, and each short video had one job.


**Number the steps and keep the counter on screen.** A row of boxes that fills in as the video moves tells the viewer where they are and how much is left. Give each step one verb, like "Isolate every source", short enough to print on the tag.


**Show the hazard at the moment it matters.** "Springs and gravity count too" lands harder on the frame where the spring is visible than in a list at the end.


**Finish with a situation the steps don't cover.** Say a colleague's lock is still on. Showing who's allowed to remove it teaches the judgment the steps leave out.


*Lockout/tagout in six steps: a sample made in Clueso for a fictional manufacturer, in isometric 3D. A counter for the six steps stays pinned to the corner. At the end, the video asks what to do when a colleague's lock is still on.*


## How do you make a policy video accessible to everyone who has to follow it?


Turn[captions](https://www.clueso.io/features/video-captions) on by default. Anyone watching on a shop floor or with the sound off gets the policy from the captions or not at all.[WCAG lists captions for prerecorded video](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/captions-prerecorded.html) as a Level A requirement.


Translate the whole frame, not only the voice. In an animated explainer the labels are text you added rather than a captured screen, so they can be translated with the narration. Clueso[translates voiceover and captions into 150+ languages](https://www.clueso.io/features/auto-translate) on every plan, along with your on-screen text, and a[translation glossary](https://www.clueso.io/features/translation-glossary) on Enterprise keeps a term like "authorized person" consistent in every language.


Don't let color carry meaning alone. Pair every red "stop" and green "go" with an icon or a word, as[WCAG's use-of-color rule](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html) asks, and publish a written version beside the video for people who'd rather read.


## How do you know employees understood the new policy?


Completion data tells you who pressed play, which is what an audit asks for, and the signed acknowledgement belongs in your HRIS or LMS, as our[handbook video guide](https://www.clueso.io/blog/employee-handbook-training-videos) explains. These checks show whether people understood it.


**Ask about a decision the viewer will face.** The parental-leave sample asks "Which timeline is Tom's?" with two options on screen, and the answer shows whether someone understood who the policy covers.


**Measure the behavior two weeks later.** Pick the number the policy should move, like the share of sick days reported through the app. If it hasn't moved, check whether the last scene states the action and the date in words a viewer could repeat.


**Log the questions that come in.** If HR answers the same question five times in the first week, add a scene that answers it and publish again.


## How can Clueso turn a policy document into an animated explainer?


Clueso is the agentic video platform for businesses. You make the four decisions above, and Clueso builds the explainer from the policy PDF or Word file, a slide deck, a script, or a prompt.


1. **Give it the policy and your decisions.** Upload the document and tell Clueso in the chat what changed, who it's for, and the action with its date.
2. **Clueso drafts the video.** It writes the script from the document and builds each scene from[motion graphics](https://www.clueso.io/features/motion-graphics) and on-screen text, with[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) and captions.
3. **Edit by asking.** Tell Clueso in the chat what to change, like "strike through 2 weeks and show 4 weeks", and the[agent](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-agents) edits that scene without touching the rest. Chat editing is on every plan, and a timeline with keyframes is there for hand edits.
4. **Translate and publish.** Translate it in one click, then[embed it](https://www.clueso.io/features/embed-videos-anywhere) where people already look, or send it to your LMS as a[SCORM package](https://www.clueso.io/features/scorm-export) on Enterprise.
5. **Update it when the policy changes.** Edit the line that changed and publish again. The embed code stays the same, so every page that shows the video serves the new version.

## Frequently asked questions


### How do I communicate a new policy to employees?


Send the full policy for the record, and a 60- to 120-second explainer for the change: what's different, who it covers, what to do, and by when. Clueso builds that explainer from the policy document, with captions and translation included.


### How do I make an animated explainer video without an animator or After Effects?


Start from what you have. In Clueso you upload a document or deck, or describe the video in a prompt, and it builds the scenes with motion graphics and an AI voiceover. You refine it by telling the[Clueso agent](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-agents) what to change in the chat, on every plan, or on the timeline.


### Which AI video maker is suitable for HR policy training?


Choose by what an update costs, because HR policies change more often than the courses built around them. Clueso fits policy training that has to stay current. Our[roundup of AI video tools for compliance training](https://www.clueso.io/blog/best-ai-video-tools-for-compliance-training) compares six, including which plans include SCORM and quizzes.


### Can I turn a safety procedure PDF into a video every crew has to watch?


Yes. Clueso's[PDF to video converter](https://www.clueso.io/tools/pdf-to-video-converter) writes a short script from the document's key steps and shows them with motion graphics under an AI voiceover. To record who watched and passed, export it as SCORM with a quiz on Enterprise, and your LMS keeps the record.


Take the next policy change on your calendar and write its before-and-after sentence today, with the one action and its date. If either won't fit on one line, settle it with the policy owner before anyone makes the video.
